fetched_contents.text: Challenging microalgal vitamins for human health Abstract Background Vitamins’ deficiency in humans is an important threat worldwide and requires solutions. In the concept of natural biofactory for bioactive compounds production, microalgae represent one of the most promising targets filling many biotechnological applications, and allowing the development of an eco-sustainable production of natural bioactive metabolites. Vitamins are probably one of the cutting edges of microalgal diversity compounds. Main text Microalgae can usefully provide many of the required vitamins in humans, more than terrestrial plants, for instance. Indeed, vitamins D and K, little present in many plants or fruits, are instead available from microalgae. The same occurs for some vitamins B (B12, B9, B6), while the other vitamins (A, C, D, E) are also provided by microalgae. This large panel of vitamins diversity in microalgal cells represents an exploitable platform in order to use them as natural vitamins’ producers for human consumption. This study aims to provide an integrative overview on vitamins content in the microalgal realm, and discuss on the great potential of microalgae as sources of different forms of vitamins to be included as functional ingredients in food or nutraceuticals for the human health. We report on the biological roles of vitamins in microalgae, the current knowledge on their modulation by environmental or biological forcing and on the biological activity of the different vitamins in human metabolism and health protection. Conclusion Finally, we critically discuss the challenges for promoting microalgae as a relevant source of vitamins, further enhancing the interests of microalgal “biofactory” for biotechnological applications, such as in nutraceuticals or cosmeceuticals. Keywords: Vitamin D, Vitamin K, Microalgae, Biotechnology, Antioxidants, Nutraceuticals Background The class of vitamins includes a diversity of organic compounds that represent essential micro-nutrients for life. These molecules cover a plethora of biological functions, such as coenzymes, hormones, antioxidants, mediators of cell signalling and regulators of cell and tissue growth or differentiation. Vitamins can be divided in two large groups, the water-soluble and fat-soluble compounds. Vitamins A, D, E and K are the four fat-soluble molecules, while the vitamin C and the vitamins B [B1 (thiamin), B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin = nicotinic acid), B5 (pantothenic acid), B6 (pyridoxine), B7 (biotin), B9 (folic acid) and B12 (cobalamin)] are water-soluble. Most of the vitamins are synthetized by photosynthetic organisms, while others (some vitamins B and vitamin K) are bioaccumulated through diet and mainly produced by bacteria [1]. Accumulation and/or synthesis of vitamins in photosynthetic organisms is highly variable [2], and strongly related to physiological responses to environmental cues [3]; the magnitude of these responses being dependent on the fitness between organism and the environment [4]. Although crucial for life, vitamins are either not or little synthetized in animals and humans, thus requiring their continuous assimilation through diet, e.g. from plants, fruits or seeds. In order to avoid vitamins deficit in humans, it is strongly recommended to follow diets with high content in the different vitamins. However, not all plants contain all vitamins, and some of them (vitamins D, K or some B) are scarcely present. Among plant kingdom, marine algae produce or/and accumulate a large diversity of vitamins (Fig. 1), and microalgae—photosynthetic unicellular and fast dividing rate organisms—potentially could be extremely helpful as vitamins’ producers, as the already known “super food” vitamins-rich Spirulina platensis [5]. Microalgae can contain vitamins such as vitamins B12 [3, 6], vitamin K [7] or D [8] that are not present in higher plants. Vitamin D is known to be highly concentrated in sea edible organisms (e.g., fishes, [9]) which accumulate it through algal based diets, being not able to synthetize it [10]. The content in the other vitamins, generally provided by higher plants, can be also significant if we consider that are unicellular organisms. For instance, the green microalga Dunaliella is known to highly accumulate the vitamins B2, B12, B9, B3 as well as the vitamins C and E [11] while high content of vitamin C has been reported in the diatom Skeletonema marinoi [12, 13]. The general aim of this study is to critically discuss if and why microalgae can become a functional source of vitamins to fill human requirements through food complements or nutraceuticals. In biotechnology, microalgae can be defined a real and natural biofactory of bioactive compounds as well as vitamins for dietary intake [14–16]. It is noteworthy that some vitamins (e.g., vitamins E, A or C) have been the object of numerous studies, although other vitamins were poorly investigated in microalgae. Here, we update an integrated state-of-art on the vitamins A, D, E, K, C, B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9 and B12 contents in microalgae, as well as on their biological roles and modulation by environmental or biological forcing in microalgae. We also report on the biological activity of the different vitamins in human metabolism and health protection. Functions and roles of vitamins in microalgae In living organisms, vitamins are involved in numerous processes and functions, being required for example as precursors or coenzymes in key metabolic pathways, controlling and regulating tissue growth and cell functioning, or acting as antioxidants. fetched_contents.text: Elemental Composition of Algae-Based Supplements by Energy Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence Abstract The aim of this study is to evaluate the elemental composition of fifteen algae-based supplements commonly sold in the Portuguese market, by energy dispersive X-ray fluorescence. Despite the fact that the majority of Kelp samples were a good source of iodine, the levels observed might well contribute to an excess in the human body, which can cause dysfunction of the thyroid gland. Furthermore, the presence of lead in Sea spaghetti, Arame, Hijiki and Wakame caused a considerable risk to public health vis a vis possible ingestion of a high daily dose. Regarding arsenic, great variability was observed in all the samples with concentrations equal to or above 60 μg/g in the case of Arame, KelpJ and Hijiki. Although algae mainly accumulate organic arsenic, some also contain high levels of its inorganic form, as is commonly pointed out for Hijiki. Thus, regular ingestion of these supplements must also take into account the mentioned facts. There is no doubt that these supplements are also good sources of other nutrients, but the lack of accurate regulations and control should alert consumers to avoid indiscriminate use of these types of products. Keywords: algae, elemental composition, food supplements, risk assessment, X-ray fluorescence 1. Introduction The use of algae as a staple food has a millenary tradition in the East, mainly in Asian countries. In Japan, over 20 species of red, green and brown algae (seaweed) are included in meals [1], with emphasis on the three most popular seaweed products—nori (Porphyra), wakame (Undaria) and kombu (Laminaria), with the first two commonly used in the preparation of sushi. However, other types of processed algae are commercialized in Asia such as gim snack (seasoned laver), mareun-gim (dried laver), okazu nori (laver for side dish), yakinori (roasted laver) and zicai tang (laver soup), with South Korea, China and Japan producing almost 100% of the total global quantity in 2017 [2]—lavers are a red seaweed species mainly from the genera Porphyra and Pyropia. The ancient use of algae dates back to before the domestication of most common animals and plants. For example, the discovery of remnants of eleven species of algae, including partially burned or squashed fragments on stone tools in South Chile, shows that human exploitation and consumption began at least 14,600 years ago [3]. Currently, in several western countries, there is an increasing acceptance of this type of food, not only in vegan and vegetarian diets, often based on the belief that both better health and disease prevention can be achieved using these “natural products” regularly, with emphasis on their intrinsic composition and abundance of several nutrients such as iodine, calcium, iron, potassium or the presence of carbohydrates, proteins, antioxidants and fiber, among others. Nevertheless, the variability of nutritional composition is hugely dependent on the geographical location and the season of collection, beyond the differences within the species, thus decisively influencing their nutritional value [4]. Additionally, studies in drug research have indicated algae as an interesting source to provide novel drugs to treat several diseases, as shown by the commercial application of the most explored chemicals from algae such as terpenes, phenols, quinones, alkaloids, lipids and other related metabolites [5]. When examining the effects of consuming Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, it was observed that algae improve human gastrointestinal issues associated with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) such as diarrhea, gas and bloating [6]. Within the variety of bioactive compounds of brown seaweeds, phloroglucinol, fucoxanthin and fucoidan are among the most abundant, also exhibiting anticancer activity. Antioxidant activity, inhibition of cell proliferation, induction of cell death and suppression of both metastasis and angiogenesis are some of the anticancer mechanisms recognized [7]. In the same context, it was concluded that fucoidan isolated from Laminaria japonica exhibited significantly higher superoxide radical scavenging activities as compared to BHA, BHT, and α-tocopherol [8], thus suggesting that fucoidan is an excellent natural antioxidant and has great potential for preventing free-radical-mediated diseases. Chemical analysis and FTIR spectra revealed the presence of a predominant iota-carrageenan in Solieria chordalis (Rhodophyceae) extracted by conventional and microwave-assisted methods. Evaluation of the antiviral activity of iota-carrageenan against HSV-1 (Herpes simplex virus Type 1) showed strong antiviral activity comparable to that verified by the use of the reference drug acyclovir, when carrageenan was extracted by a microwave-assisted method [9]. Despite the huge amount of data emphasizing the importance of natural compounds extracted from algae, several studies also point out the presence of several contaminants in algae-based supplements [10,11,12], which can invalidate the healthy benefits and preventive effects on humans. Introduction Click to copy section linkSection link copied! ---------------------------------------- Across Europe, the blue bioeconomy is gaining momentum through a growing network of marine biorefineries and strategic research initiatives. As of 2024, there are approximately 35 biorefineries in Europe utilizing marine feedstocks, with over half in commercial operation and the remainder in pilot or research phases. A recent portfolio analysis by the Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA) highlights the diversity of EU-funded algae projects, spanning the Horizon 2020, Horizon Europe, EMFF, EMFAF, and LIFE programs. (1) These efforts reflect a coordinated push to scale up marine biorefining capacity, reduce reliance on fossil-based inputs, and unlock the full potential of ocean-derived resources in line with the European Green Deal. (2) Despite the extensive research and numerous patents on microalgae and seaweed extraction, it remains crucial to continue investigating marine feedstocks, making processes more cost-effective and scalable. With the increasing demand for sustainable food sources and the need to address issues like nano- and microplastic pollution, microalgae and seaweed offer promising solutions due to the rapid growth rates and ability to be cultivated in various environments, which make them ideal candidates for sustainable and circular production. (3) Numerous studies have explored the efficacy of rapid extraction methods for isolating valuable compounds from microalgae and seaweed. Supercritical extraction, particularly using supercritical carbon dioxide (SFE-CO2), has been shown to effectively extract neutral lipids, antioxidants, and other bioactive compounds, with the extraction efficiency highly dependent on parameters such as pressure, temperature, and CO2/algae mass ratio (4) and pretreatment processes such as blanching, milling, drying, etc. (5) This method is praised for its ability to produce high-purity extracts without the use of toxic solvents. (6) SFE has shown promise in improving the yield and quality of extracts, although they require careful optimization of the operational parameters to maximize efficiency and selectivity. Microalgae, known for their high lipid content, are particularly suited for SFE using CO2, which efficiently extracts neutral lipids and antioxidants. (7) Seaweeds benefit from SFE, as it can extract a wide range of bioactive compounds, including polyunsaturated fatty acids, pigments, and antioxidants. (8) The adaptability of SFE to different types of algae and its ability to operate under mild conditions make it an attractive method for obtaining high-quality extracts from these aquatic organisms. However, the diverse and complex nature of microalgae and seaweed biomasses makes it challenging to optimize extraction parameters for different species. This complexity arises from the vast variability in the biochemical composition of marine plants due to environmental factors such as light, temperature, and nutrient availability, affecting the efficiency of extraction methods. (9) Additionally, the presence of various bioactive compounds with different polarities and solubilities complicates the selective extraction of target compounds without coextracting unwanted substances leading sometimes to multistaged extraction using different solvents and process conditions. (10) Despite the hexane efficiency, the use of this nonpolar solvent is declining due to its environmental and health risks. (11) In contrast, supercritical fluid extraction (SFE) employs safer and greener solvents, with supercritical CO2 being the most common. However, the widespread adoption of SFE is still limited by its high operational costs and the need for specialized equipment, which poses significant barriers to industrial-scale implementation. (12) Recently, water as a part of supercritical water extraction (SWE) has also gained attention as an environmentally friendly medium. SWE is known for being eco-friendly and effective for polar and nonpolar compounds, but it requires high temperatures and pressures, which can degrade heat-sensitive compounds and increase costs. (13) Mixtures of water–ethanol have been widely used for their versatility, but the challenges of managing extraction conditions and safety concerns with ethanol persist. (14) However, each of the lignocellulosic components of marine plants has its own temperature of activation and a certain time for transition to a water-soluble form convenient for isolation requiring a multiple step processing. (15) Another challenge is related to the number and complexity of extracted compounds requiring novel chemical identification approaches that can provide the reliable and comprehensive structural data of extracts. To enhance the analysis and characterization of extracted compounds, integration of a Fourier Transform Ion Cyclotron Resonance mass spectrometer (FT-ICR-MS) can be highly beneficial. FT-ICR-MS offers ultrahigh resolution and mass accuracy, making it ideal for identifying and quantifying complex mixtures of bioactive compounds extracted from microalgae and seaweed that are useful in optimizing extraction parameters and ensuring the purity and quality of the final products. Mini-report on factors affecting vitamin content in macroalgae

The evidence supports a view of macroalgae vitamin content as highly variable and sensitive to cultivation, extraction, and analytical conditions. First, cultivation conditions can alter vitamin levels, but the provided evidence does not directly quantify the extent of this effect for individual vitamins. Instead, it emphasizes that macroalgae cultivation is an active area of scientific interest and that nutrient absorption and environmental factors influence algae biomass composition [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that macroalgae farming can affect dissolved oxygen, pH, and nutrient dynamics, which may indirectly influence biochemical composition [N3-R4]. However, the provided excerpts do not give a precise mechanism for how cultivation conditions alter vitamin levels, so any claims about specific vitamin changes should be treated cautiously.

Methodological differences are a more concrete explanation for inconsistent results. The extraction-method literature explicitly states that macroalgal biomasses are chemically complex and that different compounds vary in polarity and solubility, making selective extraction difficult without coextracting unwanted substances [N5-F4]. It also notes that extraction efficiency depends on environmental factors such as light, temperature, and nutrient availability [N5-F4], and that the diverse biochemical composition of marine plants complicates the optimization of extraction parameters [N5-F4]. Additionally, the same source describes multiple extraction approaches, including supercritical fluid extraction, water–ethanol mixtures, and conventional methods, with each having different solubility, ionization, and equipment requirements [N5-F4]. These methodological differences likely explain why vitamin content can appear inconsistent across studies.

Extraction and analytical methods clearly influence reported content. The evidence shows that the choice of solvent, temperature, pressure, and pretreatment affects extraction efficiency [N5-F4]. It also highlights that high-resolution mass spectrometry can reveal species-specific molecular diversity, but biases from solubility and ionization can impede complete characterization of algal extracts [N5-F4]. This is important for vitamin reporting because it suggests that reported levels may reflect extraction success rather than absolute biological content. The same source also notes that supercritical CO2 and supercritical water extraction are environmentally friendly but still require careful optimization and may not be universally applicable across species [N5-F4].

Lipid or cell-wall composition likely affects extraction and detection. The evidence explicitly states that microalgae and seaweed biomasses have diverse and complex biochemical compositions, and that the presence of various bioactive compounds with different polarities and solubilities complicates selective extraction [N5-F4]. It also notes that SFE is particularly suited for extracting neutral lipids, antioxidants, and other bioactive compounds, while seaweeds benefit from SFE because it can extract a wide range of bioactive compounds [N5-F4]. This implies that lipid-rich algae may be easier to extract using lipid-friendly solvents, whereas cell-wall barriers or high cell-wall content may reduce extraction efficiency and lead to underestimation of some compounds. The evidence does not directly compare lipid content across algae types, so this remains an indirect inference rather than a firm conclusion.

Overall, the most defensible conclusion from the provided evidence is that vitamin content in macroalgae is shaped by cultivation conditions, extraction protocols, analytical methods, and biochemical composition, with lipid and cell-wall properties especially likely to influence recovery and detection [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-F4].

The evidence points to a broad but uneven pattern of vitamin reporting across marine macroalgae. Most frequently reported are water-soluble vitamins, especially B12, folate, niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, biotin, and vitamin C, plus some fat-soluble vitamins such as A, D, and E [N1-F3][N4-F2]. The microalgae review explicitly says that microalgae commonly provide vitamins B12, B9, B6, and also vitamins A, C, D, E, and K [N1-F3]. It also states that vitamins D and K are less present in many plants but more available from microalgae, and that some B vitamins are also more readily available from microalgae than from terrestrial plants [N1-F3]. The seaweed systematic review similarly reports seaweeds as sources of water- and fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamins A, C, D, and E, thiamin, niacin, folate, and B12 [N1-R4]. The CEVA nutritional data sheets indicate that the main edible macroalgae species covered include Spirulina, Chlorella, and two marine plants, with average content provided for each nutrient [N4-F2]. This suggests that the reported vitamins are not limited to a single species or genus, but are commonly associated with macroalgae in general.

Taxonomically restricted vitamins are more difficult to identify from the evidence provided, because the excerpts do not give a clear list of algae-specific vitamins by taxonomic group. However, the evidence does suggest some group-level associations. The seaweed review says brown macroalgae are discussed in the context of bioactive compounds [N4-R4], but the excerpts do not directly name a vitamin that is uniquely restricted to brown algae. The CEVA data sheet list includes brown, red, and green algae species, but the excerpt does not provide vitamin-specific taxonomic restriction claims [N4-F2]. The B12 literature is more informative: one seaweed study reports true vitamin B12 in seaweed and a derived protein ingredient, and notes that sea lettuce (but not dulse or sugar kelp) qualifies for a B12 nutritional EU claim [N4-R5]. This implies that B12 is not universally present across all algae, but appears in some species and may be more strongly reported in certain types of seaweed. The evidence also notes that B12 is sometimes bioaccumulated through diet rather than synthesized by algae, and that some algae may contain B12-like compounds [N1-F3], which suggests that B12 is a special case rather than a taxonomically universal vitamin.

Consistently reported vitamins are those that appear across multiple sources. These include B12, folate, niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, biotin, vitamin C, and some fat-soluble vitamins such as A, D, and E [N1-F3][N1-R4][N4-R5]. The evidence is thinner for some vitamins, particularly B12 and other less commonly studied vitamins. The microalgae review notes that some vitamins, such as vitamins E, A, or C, have been the object of numerous studies, while other vitamins were poorly investigated [N1-F3]. The seaweed systematic review similarly reports seaweeds as sources of several vitamins but does not indicate that all vitamins are consistently studied [N1-R4]. The CEVA data sheets cover main edible macroalgae species but do not provide a vitamin-by-species table in the excerpted content, so their evidence is more useful for identifying which vitamins are commonly reported than for determining which are consistently measured across all species [N4-F2].

B12 is clearly a special case. The evidence shows that it can appear in seaweed and that sea lettuce qualifies for a B12 nutritional claim [N4-R5]. It also states that B12 is sometimes bioaccumulated through diet and that some algae may contain B12-like compounds [N1-F3]. However, the evidence does not support a universal presence of true B12 across all macroalgae; instead, it suggests that B12 is species-specific and that claims should be made cautiously [N4-R5]. The B12 literature is therefore best treated as a special case with species-specific claims rather than a general macroalgae vitamin [N1-F3][N4-R5].

In summary, the most common vitamins reported in marine macroalgae are B12, folate, niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, biotin, vitamin C, and some fat-soluble vitamins such as A, D, and E [N1-F3][N1-R4]. B12 is a special case with species-specific claims, while taxonomically restricted vitamins are not clearly established in the provided evidence [N4-R5]. The evidence is stronger for consistently reported vitamins than for all possible vitamins, and B12 stands out as a particularly contested and species-dependent example [N1-F3][N4-R5].

## Summary

The evidence shows that marine macroalgae contain a range of vitamins, with B12, folate, niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, biotin, vitamin C, and some fat-soluble vitamins such as A, D, and E being the most frequently reported [N1-F3][N1-R4]. B12 is a special case because it appears in some seaweed species and is species-specific, while other vitamins are consistently reported across species and groups [N1-F3][N4-R5]. Vitamin content also varies by algae type, but the differences are not uniform across all vitamins: green, red, and brown algae differ in overall composition, and lipid-rich algae may differ from non-lipid-rich algae because of extraction challenges and cell-wall barriers [N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-F4]. Species identity within a taxonomic group is a major source of variation, and brown algae may have special features such as B12-like activity or other lipid-associated differences, though the evidence does not provide a comprehensive vitamin-by-type comparison [N4-R4][N4-R5]. Overall, vitamin content in marine macroalgae is shaped by biology, cultivation, extraction, and analytical conditions [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N5-F4].

## Which vitamins are found in marine macroalgae?

The evidence points to a broad but uneven pattern of vitamin reporting. The most frequently reported vitamins are the water-soluble B vitamins and vitamin C, along with some fat-soluble vitamins:

- **B12**: reported in seaweed and sea lettuce, but only in some species and not universally [N4-R5].
- **Folate**: reported as a common vitamin in seaweeds and in microalgae [N1-F3][N1-R4].
- **Niacin**: reported in seaweeds and microalgae [N1-F3][N1-R4].
- **Riboflavin**: reported in seaweeds and microalgae [N1-F3][N1-R4].
- **Thiamine (B1)**: reported in seaweeds and microalgae [N1-F3][N1-R4].
- **Biotin**: reported in seaweeds and microalgae [N1-F3][N1-R4].
- **Vitamin C**: reported in seaweeds and microalgae [N1-F3][N1-R4].
- **Fat-soluble vitamins**: vitamins A, D, and E are reported in seaweeds and microalgae [N1-F3][N1-R4].

The evidence also notes that vitamins D and K are less present in many plants but more available from microalgae, and that some B vitamins are more readily available from microalgae than from terrestrial plants [N1-F3]. The seaweed systematic review explicitly states that seaweeds have the potential to enhance daily vitamin intake, particularly for B12, C, and carotenoids, but it does not list all vitamins equally [N1-R4]. ## Which vitamins are taxonomically restricted to certain algae groups?

The evidence does not clearly establish a set of vitamins that are uniquely restricted to one algae group. However, it does support the idea that some vitamins appear more frequently or more strongly in particular species and genera. The most important taxonomic pattern in the evidence is that **B12 is not universal across all macroalgae**; it appears in some seaweed species and is species-specific [N4-R5]. The evidence also notes that B12 is sometimes bioaccumulated through diet rather than synthesized by algae, and that some algae may contain B12-like compounds [N1-F3]. This makes B12 a special case rather than a taxonomically universal vitamin.

For other vitamins, the evidence suggests broad availability across macroalgae, but it does not provide a complete list of algae-specific vitamins by taxonomic group. The brown macroalgae review focuses on bioactive compounds rather than vitamins, but it indicates that brown algae are discussed in the context of nutrition and health [N4-R4]. The CEVA data sheets cover brown, red, and green algae species, but the excerpt does not provide vitamin-specific taxonomic restriction claims [N4-F2]. Therefore, the evidence supports cautious generalization: some vitamins are commonly found across macroalgae, while B12 is a special case with species-specific claims [N1-F3][N4-R5].
